title: Mission-Critical Evals at Scale (Learnings from 100k medical decisions)

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's central object is evaluation methodology—reference-free evals, LLM-as-judge, and confidence estimation for measuring AI quality at scale. The application is mission-critical healthcare prior authorization within enterprise insurance operations covering 50 million American lives. The system is already in production and the talk focuses on scaling evaluation beyond MVP-stage approaches. Prerequisites assume basic familiarity with LLM products and evaluation concepts, targeting intermediate practitioners. A structured conference presentation with slides, architecture diagrams, and real-world production case examples. Includes specific production metrics, an F1 score of nearly 96%, and architecture from an operating system serving 50 million lives.

summary: Christopher Lovejoy introduces the challenge of building evaluation systems for mission-critical LLM applications in healthcare, drawing on 18 months of experience at Anterior, which serves insurance providers covering 50 million American lives. The core product supports prior authorization decisions—whether a treatment should be approved or escalated for clinician review. He illustrates how subtle medical nuance errors (e.g., calling a confirmed MS diagnosis 'suspicious') may occur infrequently but become significant at scale, with organizations facing lawsuits for inappropriate AI automation. The first approach—human reviews via an internal dashboard called 'scalp'—works at MVP scale but fails to scale: reviewing 50% of 1,000 daily decisions needs 5 clinicians, but the same ratio at 100,000 decisions needs 50. Reducing review percentage doesn't solve this because volume growth outpaces it. Offline eval datasets built from human-generated ground truths are useful for tracking performance over time but are insufficient alone because new edge cases appear before they're captured in downstream datasets—relying only on offline evals is 'playing with fire.' The solution is real-time, reference-free (label-free) evaluation, which scores outputs before knowing true outcomes. Using LLM-as-judge and confidence estimation methods, the system produces confidence gradings from high confidence to actively thinking the output is wrong. These scores enable two key functions: estimating performance across all cases (not just reviewed ones) and dynamically prioritizing human review by combining confidence with contextual factors like procedure cost, bias risk, and previous error rates. This creates a 'validating the validator' virtuous cycle where human reviews validate the reference-free evals, which in turn surface the most relevant cases for human review. Over time, unseen edge cases shrink and detection improves, building something hard to replicate without high-volume real data and iterative refinement. Once confident, the system integrates into the pipeline itself—confident outputs go to customers, uncertain ones route to more expensive models, internal clinicians, or customer review dashboards. Lovejoy distills three guiding principles: (1) build a system, not just use review data to audit performance but to improve the evaluation system itself; (2) evaluate on live production data rather than relying on offline evals, identifying problems immediately for quick response; (3) get the best reviewers and empower them, prioritizing review quality over quantity and building custom tooling to move faster. Results include avoiding massive clinical hiring (competitor has 800+ nurses vs. Anterior's <10), achieving a recent F1 score of nearly 96% in a study, and earning strong customer trust—with one nurse expressing relief at being able to keep using Anterior's AI (named Florence). The system enables real-time performance estimates, scalability at low cost, and fast response to errors while meeting customer SLAs.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.summary: Christopher Lovejoy introduces himself as a medical doctor turned AI engineer at Anterior, which serves insurance providers covering 50 million American lives. He frames the talk around building eval systems for mission-critical healthcare decisions where there's no room for error.

sections.title: Scale Challenges and Medical Example
sections.summary: Explains how going from MVP to scale reveals unseen edge cases. Uses a prior authorization example where the AI incorrectly labels a confirmed MS diagnosis as 'suspicious,' missing key medical nuance. Notes organizations are being sued for inappropriate AI automation in healthcare.

sections.title: Human Reviews and Scalability Problem
sections.summary: Describes Anterior's human review dashboard 'scalp' and the process of generating critiques and ground truths. Demonstrates that human review doesn't scale: 50% review of 1,000 decisions needs 5 clinicians, but at 100,000 decisions even 5% review needs 50 clinicians. Identifies two key questions: which cases to review and how unreviewed cases performed.

sections.title: Offline Eval Datasets
sections.summary: Discusses offline eval datasets built from human-generated ground truths, segmented by enterprise, medical type, conditions, and complexity. Notes these are useful for tracking performance over time and iterating AI pipelines, but relying only on offline evals is 'playing with fire' because new edge cases appear before being captured.

sections.title: Real-Time Reference-Free Evaluation Solution
sections.summary: Introduces real-time, reference-free evaluation using LLM-as-judge and confidence estimation to produce confidence gradings. Explains how these enable performance estimation across all cases, alignment computation with human reviews, and dynamic prioritization for human review. Describes the 'validating the validator' virtuous cycle, pipeline integration with automated routing, and impact: competitor's 800+ nurses vs. Anterior's <10 clinical experts, with AI-human alignment comparable to human-human alignment.

sections.title: Impact, Principles, and Conclusion
sections.summary: Describes how the system enables quick error correction while meeting customer SLAs, with industry-leading F1 score of nearly 96%. Customer trust is strong—one nurse expressed relief at keeping Anterior's AI (Florence). Lovejoy shares three guiding principles: (1) build a system that uses review data to improve the evaluation system itself, (2) evaluate on live production data instead of relying on offline evals, (3) get the best reviewers and empower them with quality over quantity and custom tooling. Concludes that the system provides real-time, accurate, scalable, low-cost performance estimates powered by a small expert team, and invites contact and applications for open roles.
